title: Chapter 55 — Of the Monstrous Pictures of Whales
paragraphs: Before long I shall paint for you, as well as one can without canvas, something like the true form of the whale as he actually appears to the eye of the whaleman when the whale is moored alongside the whale-ship and can fairly be stepped upon. It may be worthwhile, therefore, to first consider those curious imaginary portraits of him which even down to the present day confidently challenge the belief of the landsman. It is time to set the world right on this point. And I have no doubt the world will agree to be set right.

It may be that the original source of all those visual distortions can be found among the oldest Hindu, Egyptian, and Greek sculptures. Ever since those inventive but unscrupulous times when on the marble panels of temples, the bases of statues, and on shields, medallions, cups, and coins, the dolphin was drawn in chain-armor scales like Saladin's, and with a helmeted head like St. George's — ever since then, the same sort of license has prevailed, not only in most popular pictures of the whale, but in many supposedly scientific ones as well.

Now, by far the most ancient existing portrait purporting to be of the whale is found in the famous cave-temple of Elephanta, in India. The Brahmins maintain that in the almost endless sculptures of that ancient temple, all the trades and occupations, every conceivable pursuit of man, were depicted ages before any of them actually came into being. No wonder, then, that our noble profession of whaling should have been foreshadowed there. The Hindu whale referred to occurs in a separate sculpture panel, showing the incarnation of Vishnu in the form of the Leviathan, a creature called Matse. But though this sculpture is half man and half whale, it still does not satisfy expectations. The Hindu whale has no resemblance to the real thing.

But go to the old galleries and look at a great Christian painter's portrait of this fish, for he succeeds no better than the ancient Hindu. It is Guido's picture of Perseus rescuing Andromeda from the sea-monster or whale. Where did Guido get the model for such a strange creature? Nor does Hogarth, in painting the same scene in his own "Perseus Descending," do any better. The huge fat body of that Hogarthian monster undulates on the surface, scarcely drawing one inch of water. It has a head like a dog, and is spouting water upward from his forehead like a fountain in the park. Truly, these things are no more than signs and symbols — not real portraits of the whale.

In the illustrations and other decorations of some ancient books, you will at times encounter very curious depictions of the whale, where all manner of spouts, jets, hot springs and cold, come bubbling up from his inexhaustible brain. In the title-page of the original edition of the Advancement of Learning, you will find some curious whales.

But leaving all these amateur attempts, let us look at those pictures of whales that claim to be sober, scientific drawings, by those who know. In old Harris's collection of voyages there are some plates of whales taken from a Dutch book of voyages, published in 1671, entitled "A Whaling Voyage to Spitsbergen in the ship Jonas in the Whale, Peter Peterson of Friesland, master." In one of those plates the whales, like great rafts of logs, are shown lying among icebergs, with white bears running over their backs. In another plate, the prodigious blunder is made of giving the whale eyes the size of a man's head — and even those are set in the wrong part of the head.

Then again, there is an imposing volume written by one Captain Colnett, a Post Captain in the English navy, entitled "A Voyage round Cape Horn into the South Seas, for the purpose of extending the Spermaceti Whale Fisheries." In this book is an outline claiming to be a "Picture of a Spermaceti whale, drawn by scale from one killed on the coast of Mexico, August, 1793, and hoisted on deck." I have no doubt the captain had this faithful picture made for the benefit of his marines. To anyone who studies it, the whale in question looks much like an overgrown Guinea pig. Of course, he is a great deal worse than that.

Nor are the most careful compilations of Natural History for the education of the young and innocent free from the same kind of blunder. Look at that popular work Goldsmith's Animated Nature. In the abridged London edition of 1807, there are plates of an alleged "whale" and a "narwhal." I do not wish to seem rude, but this unsightly whale looks much like an amputated sow. And as for the narwhal, one glance is enough to astonish anyone that in this nineteenth century such a thing could be presented to students as truth.

Then again, in 1825, Bernard Germain, Count de Lacepede, a great naturalist, published a scientific whale book with several pictures of the different species of whale. All of these are not only incorrect, but the picture of the Right Whale — even Scoresby, a long-experienced man in that species — declares has no counterpart in nature.

But the crowning achievement of all this blundering was reserved for the scientific Frederick Cuvier, brother of the famous Baron. In 1836 he published a Natural History of Whales, in which he gives what he calls a picture of the Sperm Whale. Before showing that picture to any Nantucketer, you had better plan your quick escape from Nantucket. In a word, Frederick Cuvier's Sperm Whale is not a Sperm Whale, but a squash. Of course, he never had the benefit of a whaling voyage — which is how most of these one-sided scientific portraits of the whale are produced.

As for the sign-painters' whales seen in the streets, hanging over the shops of oil-dealers — what shall be said of them? They are generally monstrous whales with camel humps and very savage expressions, breakfasting on three or four boatloads of sailors. Their deformities flounder in seas of blood and blue paint.

But these many mistakes in depicting the whale are not so very surprising after all. Consider: most of the scientific drawings have been made from stranded fish. And these are about as accurate as a drawing of a wrecked ship, with its back broken, would be in correctly representing the noble vessel in all its full pride of hull and mast. Though elephants have stood for their full-length portraits, the living whale has never yet properly posed for his. The living whale, in his full majesty and significance, is only to be seen at sea in unfathomable waters. And in the great majority of cases, the hunter's first sight of the whale is from a considerable distance.

But it may be imagined that from the naked skeleton of a stranded whale, accurate hints might be gathered about his true form. Not at all. For it is one of the more curious things about this creature that his skeleton gives very little idea of his general shape. Though Jeremy Bentham's skeleton, which hangs as a chandelier in the library of one of his executors, correctly conveys the idea of a burly-browed practical old gentleman — yet the whale's skeleton could tell you nothing of that gentle curve of his back, or that blending of his body into his flukes.

For all these reasons, then, however you look at it, you must conclude that the great whale is that one creature in the world which must remain unpainted to the last. True, one portrait may come much nearer the mark than another, but none can hit it with any considerable degree of accuracy. So there is no earthly way of finding out precisely what the whale really looks like. And the only way you can get even a tolerable idea of his living shape is by going whaling yourself. But by doing so, you run no small risk of being forever stove in and sinking to the bottom. So it may go with you.
